chapter: Rhythm Club memories and playing technique
title: How Jelly Roll Morton ran his record sessions

bands.name: Jelly Roll Morton's Red Hot Peppers

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Remembering Jelly Roll Morton: the man, the band

blocks.x: Well let's see, do you know much about Ward Pinkert's association with Jelly Roll?

No I don't. I know that they had been friends for a long while, much longer than I was friends with Jelly Roll, because prior to this session that I made with him, he had been making records with Jelly Roll, so I imagine their acquaintance was long lived.
I forgot to ask you yesterday about when you were recording with Jelly Roll. How did those sessions go
in the studio? Did he have someone write arrangements for him of his tunes, and then they were brought into the studio and run down or how did it go?

Well my experience with the session I did, I think I did two. He never had anything written out. When we got to the studio he had a skeleton sheet, probably, maybe with the introduction. The rest of it was ad lib, where the boys would take choruses and he may have an out-chorus, or sometimes they would get together a riff, and after the riff they'd have about eight bar ending, and that's all I remember. Now as far as the drums were concerned, he would just tell me how many choruses that this one's going to take and if he wanted a brass figure brought up, he would tell me just what to do on it, or let me listen to it, and that's about all. They were mostly heads that he would get together right in the studio. Now everybody was accustomed to working with Jelly with the exception of me, and they knew his style and knew exactly what to expect, and that's what made his recording dates a success, because they were just ad lib things and everybody would just go on and play and the ensemble things he would maybe have just a lot of tailgate going in there, you know, and things that he would want to- gether on ensemble, he would have it written out, maybe eight bars, not too much, maybe a four bar introduction, he may have written out, eight bars. Sometimes none, because he would take the intro.
The people who were the sidemen must have been pretty fast learners.

Oh yes, they were, and they were accustomed to his work, his playing, and they had made records with him before, and then Jelly Roll see used to have a band in the dancing school at 125th and 7th Avenue, the Roseland. A lot of these guys were working with his band up there, so they knew his style, they knew exactly in which direction Jelly was going.
It was a working band, too.
Oh yes, yeah. He had a large band. Of course when he recorded, the band was, oh well, four, five, six, eight pieces sometime, different size.
Well that's interesting, the way you described it, because some of those things are more complex than just riff tunes.

Yes, they are. Well, from working together. See this Ernie Bullock, clarinet player, he was very good, of course his technique just fit what Jelly Roll was doing, and the men surrounded by him, you know, they knew just what riff he was going to play or in which direction he was going to lead them.
